sepsis.label: Septic shock / severe sepsis
sepsis.fluidStrategy: Balanced crystalloid (Hartmann/Plasmalyte) preferred over 0.9% saline (SSC 2026 — except TBI use NS). 30 mL/kg suggested but with greater emphasis on individualization and dynamic measures (PLR, SVV, capillary refill). Fluid removal/de-resuscitation now addressed once stable.
sepsis.vasopressor: Noradrenaline first-line. Start peripherally — do NOT delay for central access (SSC 2026). Target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg general, but MAP 60-65 in adults ≥ 65 years (SSC 2026). Steroids suggested for refractory shock.
sepsis.screening: NEWS/MEWS now preferred over qSOFA for screening (SSC 2026 — qSOFA had poor sensitivity)
sepsis.lactateNote: Elevated lactate should NOT trigger reflexive fluid administration — multifactorial causes (stress response, mitochondrial dysfunction, hepatic clearance). Use serial lactate as adjunct, not sole driver.
sepsis.bicarbAdvice: Bicarbonate not routinely recommended in sepsis-induced lactic acidosis (SSC 2026); consider only if pH < 7.10 with AKI (BICAR-ICU subgroup)
sepsis.antimicrobials: Septic shock: antibiotics within 1 h. Probable sepsis without shock: within 1 h. Possible sepsis low-risk: defer + monitor (SSC 2026).
sepsis.referenceCitation: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 — Critical Care Medicine April 2026 (DOI 10.1097/CCM.0000000000007075); 129 recommendations replacing SSC 2021

dka.label: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
dka.glucoseTarget: 8–12 mmol/L (144–216 mg/dL) initially; switch to 5% dextrose when glucose < 14
dka.insulinDose: Insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h IV (do NOT bolus in paeds; consider 0.05 U/kg/h in adults)
dka.fluidProtocol: 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 h, then per protocol; switch to dextrose-saline when glucose < 14 mmol/L
dka.potassiumProtocol: Potassium replacement when K⁺ < 5.5 mmol/L (40 mmol/L of fluid). HOLD insulin if K⁺ < 3.3.
dka.bicarbAdvice: Sodium bicarbonate NOT recommended unless pH < 6.9 (no benefit, may worsen cerebral oedema risk in paeds). ADA 2026: bicarbonate use generally not recommended (no difference in resolution time).
dka.cerebralEdemaRisk: Watch for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA — slow rehydration, mannitol if signs
dka.euglycemicDKA: Euglycemic DKA: low insulin levels with reduced food intake, pregnancy, alcohol use, liver failure, SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. Consider when ketosis present despite glucose < 14 mmol/L (ADA 2026).
dka.referenceCitation: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Diabetes Care 49 Suppl 1:S339, Jan 2026 — replaces 2024); ADA Hyperglycemic Crises Consensus 2024 (Umpierrez); JBDS-IP 2023; ISPAD 2022 (paediatric)

arrest.label: Cardiac arrest / post-ROSC
arrest.bicarbAdvice: Bicarbonate NOT routine in cardiac arrest (consider only in hyperkalaemia, TCA overdose, or pre-existing severe metabolic acidosis)
arrest.targetPaCO2: Post-ROSC: PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg (avoid both hypocapnia and hypercapnia)
arrest.targetTemp: Post-ROSC: targeted temperature management 32–36°C × 24 hours per ILCOR 2020
arrest.referenceCitation: ILCOR 2020 / ERC 2025; UK Resus Council 2025 (replaces 2021, implementing Jan 2026)

respiratory.label: Respiratory failure (COPD/asthma/ARDS)
respiratory.paCO2COPDtarget: COPD: target SpO₂ 88–92% (avoid CO₂ retention from over-oxygenation)
respiratory.nivIndications: NIV indicated if pH 7.25–7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45 in COPD exacerbation (BTS/ICS 2016, no major update since)
respiratory.intubationCriteria: Intubation if pH < 7.25 with respiratory acidosis, exhaustion, or NIV failure
respiratory.asthmaRule: In severe asthma: rising or normal PaCO₂ is a sign of EXHAUSTION — urgent escalation needed (do not be reassured by "normal" CO₂)
respiratory.copdInhalerNote: COPD with asthma overlap → mandatory ICS use (GOLD 2025). LABA+LAMA+ICS preferred over LABA+ICS when ICS indicated.
respiratory.bicarbAdvice: Bicarbonate generally not used for respiratory acidosis (correct ventilation instead)
respiratory.referenceCitation: BTS/ICS 2016 NIV; GINA 2025 asthma strategy report; GOLD 2025 COPD report (current published)

renal.label: AKI / CKD / dialysis-dependent
renal.bicarbAdvice: Bicarbonate may be used in CKD/AKI metabolic acidosis aiming HCO₃ ≥ 22 (KDIGO 2024 CKD); avoid if volume overload
renal.kManagement: Hyperkalaemia management more aggressive — early dialysis if refractory
renal.fluidStrategy: Cautious fluid resuscitation. Use balanced crystalloids; avoid hyperchloraemia (NS large-volume associated with AKI in SMART/SALT-ED). Consider RRT early if oliguric/acidotic. Stress-dose tools (NephroCheck, urine [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP-7]) where available for biomarker-guided escalation.
renal.drugAdjustment: Adjust drug doses for renal function; avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides)
renal.framework: KDIGO 2012 AKI staging remains the current published reference. Recognise AKI as a continuum (RIFLE/AKIN/KDIGO) with downstream CKD risk.
renal.referenceCitation: KDIGO 2024 CKD Clinical Practice Guideline; KDIGO 2012 AKI Clinical Practice Guideline (current published; 2026 update in development)

toxic.label: Toxic ingestion (alcohols / salicylate)
toxic.methanolAntidote: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading (or ethanol if unavailable) + folinic acid + dialysis
toxic.ethyleneGlycolAntidote: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading + thiamine + pyridoxine + dialysis
toxic.salicylateAntidote: Urinary alkalinisation (sodium bicarbonate to urine pH > 7.5) + dialysis if severe (level > 700 mg/L, AKI, pulmonary oedema, or pH < 7.20)
toxic.isopropanolAdvice: Isopropanol → ketosis without metabolic acidosis (osmolar gap raised but anion gap normal)

general.label: General / unspecified
general.bicarbAdvice: Bicarbonate considered if pH < 7.10 with haemodynamic instability; recheck ABG after 15–30 min
